stories.title: The Light in the Locked Room

pages.text: In the closing years of the tenth century, the scholars of Basra spoke of a young man named al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham with a mixture of admiration and unease. He had mastered geometry before most of his peers had finished memorising their tables, and he argued with the ancient Greeks as though they were classmates who had made careless errors. Brilliance, however, has a way of outrunning wisdom, and one evening, surrounded by eager listeners, he made a remark he would spend a decade regretting. "If I were in Egypt," he declared, "I could build works that would regulate the Nile, so that its waters would serve the people in every season, whether the flood was generous or mean." It was the kind of boast that evaporates by morning in most cities, but words travel faster than caravans, and this one reached Cairo intact. There it fell upon the ears of the Fatimid ruler al-Hakim, a man whose curiosity was matched only by his reputation for sudden and alarming changes of temper.

The summons arrived sealed and courteous, which made it all the more impossible to refuse. As the chroniclers tell it, the ruler rode out to greet the scholar at the gates of Cairo himself, an honour so lavish that Ibn al-Haytham felt it settle on his shoulders like a yoke. "They tell me you can master the river that has mastered every king before me," al-Hakim said, his gaze unnervingly steady. "I am told many things, Your Highness, and not all of them are wise," Ibn al-Haytham replied, attempting a modesty that came several months too late. The ruler laughed, though there was little warmth in it, and promised him men, money and materials without limit. By the time the young scholar retired to his lodgings that night, he understood that he had been granted everything except the freedom to fail.

He sailed south with a small company of engineers and labourers, and for the first few days his confidence held. The Nile slid past in broad, unhurried coils, and he filled page after page with calculations of gradient and volume. Yet the further they travelled, the more often the boat passed the ruins of temples whose columns rose from the sand with an almost insolent precision. "Look at the scale of it," murmured Yusuf, the young assistant who had been assigned to record his measurements. "Whoever raised those stones understood mathematics as well as anyone alive today." Ibn al-Haytham did not answer, because the same thought had already lodged itself in his mind like a splinter: if the builders of such marvels had not tamed the river, what had made him imagine that he could?

At the cataracts near Aswan, the truth stopped being a suspicion and became a wall of water. The river hurled itself through a chaos of granite boulders, roaring with a force that made every diagram in his satchel look like a child's drawing. He spent days surveying the channels, testing his figures against the current, searching for the one ingenious solution that would vindicate his promise. None existed, at least not with the knowledge and tools of his age, and he was too honest a thinker to persuade himself otherwise. "Shall I note that the site is unsuitable?" Yusuf asked quietly, his pen hovering above the page. "Note that the scholar was mistaken," Ibn al-Haytham said, and the words cost him more than any calculation he had ever made.

The journey back to Cairo was the longest of his life, for every bend in the river brought him closer to a confession that might well cost him his head. He rehearsed elaborate explanations and discarded them one by one, recognising them for what they were: attempts to equivocate rather than to tell the truth. When at last he stood before al-Hakim, he spoke plainly, admitting that the project was beyond the reach of any engineer, himself included. The court held its breath, and the silence stretched until it seemed to have a texture of its own. Against all expectation, the ruler merely waved a hand, accepted the apology and appointed him to a minor administrative post. It was a reprieve, but Ibn al-Haytham knew enough of this court to suspect that a pardon granted on a whim could be withdrawn on another.

Months passed, and the stories that drifted through Cairo's markets about the ruler's unpredictable punishments did nothing to calm his nerves. According to the old accounts, he resolved upon a desperate stratagem: he would feign madness, reasoning that a man who had lost his mind could hardly be held responsible for anything at all. Historians still debate whether this was cowardice or a shrewd act of self-preservation, and perhaps it was a little of both. Whatever its morality, the plan worked, though not without a price. His property was confiscated, his post was taken away, and he was confined to a house near the great mosque of al-Azhar, attended by servants and watched by guards. The brilliant young man who had once promised to command a river now found himself unable to command even his own front door.

For the first weeks, he simply endured the gloom, for the shutters were kept closed and the days blurred into one another. Then, one afternoon, he noticed something that thousands of people before him must have seen and dismissed without a second thought. A single beam of sunlight was entering through a tiny hole in the shutter, and on the opposite wall, faint but unmistakable, was a picture of the street outside. He could make out a passing cart, the swaying branch of a tree and the bright robe of a merchant, all rendered in miniature colour. Most astonishing of all, the entire scene was upside down. He sat motionless for a long time, scarcely daring to blink, as though the image might vanish if he startled it.

Curiosity, it turned out, was the one thing his captors could not confiscate. He persuaded a puzzled servant to bring him candles, which he arranged in a row outside a small aperture while he sat in the darkness within. "Now cover the first flame, the one on the left," he instructed, and the servant, though convinced his master was every bit as mad as people claimed, obeyed. Instantly, a spot of light on the far right of the wall disappeared. "You see?" Ibn al-Haytham exclaimed, with an energy he had not felt in months. "The light travels in straight lines, so it must cross over as it passes through the opening; nothing comes out of the eye at all, as the ancients believed. The light comes to us."

Over the following years, the locked room became a laboratory of extraordinary ambition. He studied reflection with polished mirrors and refraction with vessels of water, and he dissected the workings of the eye with a rigour that left the theories of Euclid and Ptolemy looking distinctly unsteady. Above all, he insisted that no claim deserved trust simply because of the reputation of the person who had made it. The seeker after truth, he wrote, does not place his faith in the writings of the ancients but questions them, testing every assertion against reason and careful demonstration. He turned the same suspicion upon his own work, conscious that a mind capable of boasting about the Nile was equally capable of fooling itself in other ways. In 1021, news reached the house that al-Hakim had vanished mysteriously during one of his solitary night rides, and soon afterwards, to the bewilderment of his guards, Ibn al-Haytham made a remarkable recovery.

He emerged from confinement no longer a precocious young man eager to impress, but a scholar whose ideas had been forged in a decade of solitude. The great work that grew from those years, the Book of Optics, would be copied, studied and, some two centuries later, translated into Latin, where its author became known as Alhazen. Scholars across continents built upon his methods for generations, and many historians now regard him as one of the founders of experimental science. Yet perhaps his most heroic act occurred not in the laboratory but on the banks of the river at Aswan, when he chose to admit an error rather than disguise it. It is easy to celebrate the conquerors who bend nature to their will, but rarer and harder to honour the thinker who has the courage to say, "I was wrong; now let us find out what is true." From the darkest room in Cairo, after all, came one of history's clearest explanations of light.

dialogue.t: So, do you think exams like Qudurat and Tahsili genuinely predict who will succeed at university?
It would be somewhat simplistic to claim that they predict success outright. They measure performance on a particular day, under particular pressure.

grammar.ar: تُستخدم التراكيب التنازلية للاعتراف بوجهة نظر الطرف الآخر قبل الرد عليها، مما يجعل الحجة أكثر لباقة وإقناعاً. من أهمها: Granted ثم nevertheless، وWhile I take your point that، وMuch as I appreciate التي تعني «مع تقديري لـ...»، وBe that as it may بمعنى «مهما يكن من أمر». لاحظ أن Much as تُستعمل في بداية الجملة وتأتي بعدها جملة كاملة، ولا تعني «بقدر ما» هنا بل «على الرغم من».
examples: Granted, the scheme is well-intentioned; nevertheless, its execution leaves much to be desired.
Much as I admire your conviction, I'd question whether the data support it.
Be that as it may, we cannot ignore the logistical burden on schools.

words.ar: ثنائية زائفة (حصر الخيارات في اثنين فقط خطأً)
words.ex: Saying we must choose between tradition and progress is a false dichotomy.
The claim that allowing phones in class will lead to the collapse of education is a classic slippery slope.
Judging an entire generation by a few viral videos is a hasty generalization.
There's no proven causal link between gaming and poor exam results.
His premise is presented as self-evident, yet it is highly debatable.

words.ar: دليل قائم على تجارب أو روايات فردية
words.ex: Anecdotal evidence from a handful of friends hardly constitutes proof.

dialogue.t: Here's a post I found: 'Either we ban TikTok completely, or our teenagers will lose the ability to concentrate.' What do you make of it?
To frame it as either a total ban or a lost generation is a false dichotomy. There are plenty of options in between, such as screen-time limits or digital literacy education.
Another user replied: 'My cousin uses TikTok all day and failed his exams, so the app clearly ruins students.'
There's no causal link between one cousin's app usage and his results. He might have failed for countless other reasons. It's purely anecdotal evidence.
And this one: 'If we let students use AI for homework, soon nobody will be able to write a sentence.'
That argument rests on the assumption that any use of AI inevitably leads to total dependence, which is by no means self-evident. It's a textbook slippery slope.
Last one: 'Young people today don't read anymore.'
That's a sweeping generalization that overlooks the many teenagers who read extensively, often online or in genres older people don't recognise as serious reading.

grammar.title: Evaluative Non-Defining Relative Clauses
grammar.ar: تُستخدم جملة الوصل غير المحددة التي تبدأ بـ which بعد فاصلة للتعليق على فكرة الجملة السابقة كلها وتقييمها، وليس على اسم واحد فقط. هذا الأسلوب شائع جداً في النقد الأكاديمي، مثل: which is by no means self-evident أي «وهو أمر ليس بديهياً على الإطلاق». ويمكن أيضاً استخدام that بعد الاسم لتحديد ما يتجاهله التعميم، مثل a generalization that overlooks.
examples: The author assumes that all students have internet access at home, which is by no means guaranteed.
His conclusion is drawn from a single survey, which seriously weakens his argument.
It's a claim that overlooks the role of socioeconomic background entirely.

words.ex: The medium of instruction in most Saudi medical schools is English.
A nation's linguistic heritage is inseparable from its cultural identity.
Exclusive use of English risks marginalizing Arabic in academic and scientific fields.
High proficiency in English opens doors to international research collaborations.
Over time, neglect can erode a language's capacity to express technical concepts.
English has become indispensable in global scientific publishing.

dialogue.t: You have two minutes. Should Arabic or English be the primary medium of instruction in Saudi universities?
What concerns me most is that we're treating this as a purely practical question, when it is in fact a question of identity.
Go on, but surely English is indispensable for science and research?

It is, and I don't deny that. But rarely do we consider what happens to Arabic when it's excluded from laboratories and lecture halls. Not only does it lose prestige, but it also loses the vocabulary it needs to evolve.
So you'd make Arabic the primary language?
Yes. It is precisely because Arabic has such a rich linguistic heritage that we should equip it for modern science, rather than allow it to erode.
And what about English proficiency?

Under no circumstances should we abandon English; it should be taught rigorously alongside. But only when Arabic is used for serious academic work will it remain a language of knowledge rather than merely of tradition.

grammar.title: Negative Inversion and Cleft Sentences for Emphasis
grammar.ar: القلب أو التقديم (Inversion) يحدث عندما نبدأ الجملة بتعبير نفي أو تقييد مثل Rarely وNot only وUnder no circumstances وOnly when، فيأتي الفعل المساعد قبل الفاعل كما في السؤال: Rarely do we consider. أما الجمل المشطورة (Cleft sentences) مثل What concerns me most is وIt is precisely because... that فتُستخدم لتسليط الضوء على عنصر معيّن في الجملة. يمنح هذان الأسلوبان الخطاب قوة بلاغية ونبرة رسمية مؤثرة.
examples: Seldom have policymakers paused to ask students which language they learn best in.
Only when both languages are valued equally will we produce truly bilingual graduates.
It is precisely this imbalance that worries many educators.

words.ex: Some educationalists contend that remote learning widens the achievement gap.
The ministry has adopted a cautious stance on expanding online degrees.
Despite their differences, the experts' views converge on the importance of teacher training.
Many universities have settled on a hybrid model combining online lectures with in-person seminars.
I agree with her conclusion, with one important caveat.
On balance, the advantages of the reform outweigh its drawbacks.

dialogue.t: You've read all three opinions. Could you summarize them for me?

Certainly. Whereas Dr Al-Harbi contends that remote learning offers unmatched flexibility, Professor Lewis takes a rather more cautious stance, arguing that it works only for highly self-disciplined learners.
And the third expert?
Dr Mansour is the most critical. She maintains that in-person learning is irreplaceable for social development, particularly for younger students.
Do they agree on anything at all?
Surprisingly, yes. What these views have in common is the belief that the quality of teaching matters far more than the format itself.
So where do you stand?

Taken together, these perspectives point to a hybrid model. On balance, I'm persuaded that remote learning can be highly effective, provided that it's combined with regular face-to-face interaction and proper support for less independent learners.

grammar.title: Contrasting and Synthesizing Viewpoints
grammar.ar: لتلخيص آراء متعددة نستخدم Whereas للمقارنة بين رأيين متعارضين في جملة واحدة، ونستخدم What these views have in common is لإبراز القاسم المشترك. أما Taken together فهي عبارة اسم مفعول تعني «إذا أُخذت مجتمعةً» وتمهّد للاستنتاج. وتُستخدم provided that بمعنى «بشرط أن» لوضع شرط على الرأي النهائي، ويأتي بعدها فعل في زمن المضارع حتى لو كان المعنى مستقبلياً.
examples: Whereas the first study focuses on test scores, the second examines student wellbeing.
Taken together, the findings suggest that neither format is inherently superior.
Online courses can be just as rigorous, provided that assessment is carefully designed.

words.ex: The motion before us today is both timely and deeply contentious.
Her rebuttal exposed several weaknesses in the opposition's case.

words.ar: يتغاضى عن / يمرّ سريعاً على أمر مهم
words.ex: The report glosses over the serious privacy concerns surrounding AI tools.
Fears that AI will replace all teachers are largely unfounded.
AI tutors could democratize access to high-quality support.
Universities are rewriting their policies to protect academic integrity in the age of AI.

dialogue.t: Ladies and gentlemen, I rise to propose the motion that artificial intelligence will do more harm than good to education. It threatens academic integrity and erodes students' ability to think independently.
Madam Chair, I rise to oppose the motion that AI will do more harm than good to education. Allow me to address the central claim that AI destroys independent thinking.
Please do. Students already submit essays they haven't written themselves.

My opponent has conveniently glossed over the fact that plagiarism existed long before AI. Far from destroying critical thinking, the evidence clearly indicates that well-designed AI tools can personalize feedback and push students further.
Yet not every school has the resources to design such tools responsibly.
Which is precisely why AI matters. A student in a remote village with no private tutor can now receive instant, tailored support. AI has the potential to democratize education, not degrade it.
Then I'll leave the house to weigh the risks I've outlined.
In closing, I would urge you to consider that the fears behind this motion are largely unfounded. The question is not whether AI belongs in education, but how wisely we use it. I urge you to oppose.

grammar.title: Rhetorical Contrast with 'Far from'
grammar.ar: تُستخدم العبارة Far from متبوعة باسم أو بفعل منتهٍ بـ ing للتعبير عن أن الحقيقة عكس ما يُدّعى تماماً، أي «بعيداً عن أن يكون... بل على العكس». وهي أداة قوية في المناظرات لرفض ادعاء الخصم وتقديم الحقيقة المضادة في الجملة نفسها. لاحظ أن الجملة الرئيسية بعد الفاصلة تحمل الفكرة المعاكسة، مثل: Far from harming students, AI supports them.
examples: Far from replacing teachers, AI frees them to focus on what matters most.
Far from being a passing trend, generative AI is reshaping assessment worldwide.
Far from solving the problem, the ban has simply driven AI use underground.

words.ar: منتشر في كل مكان / واسع الانتشار
words.ex: By 2050, sensors may be so ubiquitous in smart cities that residents barely notice them.
Critics warn that the erosion of privacy often happens gradually, one convenient app at a time.
The planners envisage seamless transport, where autonomous pods connect every district.
Projects like NEOM could usher in an era of carbon-neutral urban living.
There is an inevitable trade-off between personalised services and the amount of data we surrender.
Without robust safeguards, a city run by algorithms could take on a rather dystopian character.

dialogue.t: So, picture 2050. Were cities like NEOM to become widespread, we might well see the traditional commute disappear altogether.
I'd go further than that. It's not inconceivable that the very idea of an office will feel as outdated as a fax machine does now.
Perhaps, but someone still has to maintain all that infrastructure. In all likelihood, AI will have absorbed most routine jobs by the time we're middle-aged, yet new technical roles will emerge.
True. What worries me more is privacy. If every streetlight is collecting data, where exactly does convenience end and surveillance begin?
That's the trade-off, isn't it? Residents might accept it for safer streets and cleaner air, at least initially.
Initially, yes. But should the data-protection framework fail, the consequences could be severe, from identity theft to a gradual erosion of personal freedom.
Which is why transparency has to be designed in from the start, not bolted on as an afterthought.
Agreed. A smart city is only as trustworthy as the people governing its data.

grammar.title: Inverted conditionals: Were ... to / Should ...
grammar.ar: في الأسلوب الرسمي والأكاديمي يمكن حذف if وتقديم الفعل المساعد على الفاعل. نستخدم Were + الفاعل + to + المصدر للحديث عن احتمالات افتراضية أو بعيدة في المستقبل، ونستخدم Should + الفاعل + المصدر لاحتمال ممكن لكنه غير مؤكد. هذا القلب يجعل التخمين أكثر رصانة ودقة، ويشيع في الكتابة والنقاش المتقدم.
examples: Were autonomous vehicles to become the norm, urban car parks might well be converted into green spaces.
Should the power grid fail, the consequences could be catastrophic for a fully automated city.
Were governments to regulate facial recognition more strictly, public trust in smart cities would probably increase.

words.ar: تعديل الخلايا الجنسية (تعديل وراثي ينتقل إلى الأجيال القادمة)
words.ex: Germline editing raises particular concern because its effects would be inherited by future generations.
Most ethicists distinguish sharply between therapeutic interventions and genetic enhancement.
Islamic bioethics places great emphasis on the sanctity of life and the preservation of the soul.
Some scholars invoke maslaha to argue that preventing a fatal hereditary disease serves the public interest.

words.ar: منحدر زلق (خطوة صغيرة تقود إلى عواقب أخطر)
words.ex: Opponents fear a slippery slope from curing disease to designing children with preferred traits.
Many people are uneasy about scientists tampering with the human genome.

dialogue.t: Gene editing for disease prevention seems almost impossible to object to. Who wouldn't want to eliminate sickle cell anaemia?
Few would object to the aim. The crux of the matter is whether we can do it without unforeseen harm to future generations.
Well, one could argue that it's justifiable insofar as it prevents serious suffering. That aligns with the Islamic principle of preserving life, hifz al-nafs.
Absolutely, and many scholars would accept that under maslaha. But there's a fine line between treating a disease and enhancing traits like intelligence or height.
That's precisely where international guidelines become important. The WHO, for instance, has called for strict oversight of germline research.
Right. From an ethical standpoint, the key concern is consent. An embryo can't agree to changes that will be passed on indefinitely.
So perhaps somatic editing, which affects only the patient, is a more defensible starting point.
I'd say so. It respects the sanctity of life while avoiding the slippery slope towards designer babies.

grammar.title: Focusing structures with noun clauses (whether / insofar as)
grammar.ar: نستخدم عبارات مثل The crux of the matter is أو The key concern is متبوعة بجملة اسمية تبدأ بـ whether أو that لتسليط الضوء على جوهر القضية قبل عرضها. أما insofar as فتعني «بقدر ما» أو «إلى الحد الذي»، وتُستخدم لتقييد الحكم بشرط معيّن. هذه التراكيب تمنح الحجة دقة وتوازنًا في النقاش الأخلاقي.
examples: The crux of the matter is whether the benefits to patients justify the risks to future generations.
Gene therapy is justifiable insofar as it relieves genuine suffering rather than satisfying parental preference.
From an ethical standpoint, the key concern is that genetic inequality could deepen existing social divisions.

words.ex: A well-chosen analogy can make an abstract idea instantly accessible.
Good science communicators strip away jargon without distorting the science.
Once you grasp the idea of trial and error, neural networks become far less mysterious.
The article explains quantum computing in terms a layperson can follow.

words.ar: يتلخّص في / يرجع في جوهره إلى
words.ex: Ultimately, machine learning boils down to finding patterns in vast amounts of data.
It's counterintuitive, but making a network slightly 'forget' information can improve its performance.

dialogue.t: Okay, everyone keeps talking about neural networks 'learning'. But a computer can't actually learn, can it?
Not the way you do, no. Put simply, it adjusts lots of tiny numbers until its guesses get better.
Tiny numbers? That sounds even more confusing.
Fair enough. A useful way to think about it is like tuning a huge sound mixing desk with millions of knobs. Each knob controls how much attention the network pays to a particular clue.
So someone sits there turning millions of knobs?

That's the clever part. It's rather like practising penalty kicks, except that the network measures exactly how far it missed and corrects itself automatically. To unpack that a little further, after every wrong answer it nudges each knob slightly in the direction that would have reduced the error.
And it does that thousands of times?
Millions, usually. In other words, what this boils down to is extremely fast, extremely patient trial and error.

grammar.title: Analogy with qualification: It's rather like ..., except that ...
grammar.ar: عند تبسيط مفهوم معقد نستخدم تشبيهًا مألوفًا ثم نُقيّده لنوضح حدوده، فنقول It's rather like + اسم/جملة ثم except that + جملة تبيّن الفرق. كلمة rather تخفف من قوة التشبيه وتشير إلى أنه تقريبي. كما نستخدم عبارات إعادة الصياغة مثل In other words وPut simply لتلخيص الفكرة بلغة أبسط.
examples: A battery is rather like a water tank, except that it stores chemical energy instead of water.
Pumped hydro storage is rather like lifting a heavy weight, except that the weight is millions of litres of water.
In other words, what this boils down to is storing energy when it's cheap and releasing it when it's needed.

words.ex: Investment in renewables is central to the Kingdom's strategy of economic diversification under Vision 2030.
Solar power's intermittency means that reliable storage solutions are essential.
Green hydrogen could allow Saudi Arabia to remain a major energy exporter in a low-carbon world.
The high initial costs may be offset by long-term savings on fuel.

words.ar: أصول عالقة (استثمارات تفقد قيمتها قبل أوانها)
words.ex: Investors are increasingly wary of fossil fuel infrastructure becoming stranded assets.
The commercial viability of hydrogen exports depends heavily on transport costs.

dialogue.t: Thank you for joining this consultation. Overall, how would you assess the Kingdom's investment in solar and hydrogen?
On balance, I believe the potential gains far outweigh the risks. We have abundant sunshine, vast land and existing energy expertise.
Yet critics point to the enormous capital costs. Aren't those a serious concern?
They are, but they're likely to be offset by falling technology prices and new export revenues. That said, there's a considerable degree of uncertainty surrounding global hydrogen demand.
Could you elaborate on that uncertainty?

Certainly. It remains to be seen whether importing countries like Germany or Japan will build the infrastructure to receive hydrogen on a large scale. Without that, commercial viability is questionable.
And environmentally?
The long-term implications are likely to be positive, provided water use for electrolysis is managed carefully, since desalination carries its own environmental footprint.

grammar.title: Impersonal hedging structures for uncertainty
grammar.ar: في سياق السياسات والتقييم نتجنب الأحكام القاطعة باستخدام تراكيب غير شخصية مثل It remains to be seen whether (يبقى أن نرى ما إذا) وThere is a degree of uncertainty surrounding. كما نستخدم be likely to للتعبير عن احتمال مرجّح دون جزم. هذه التراكيب تُظهر الموضوعية وتجعل المتحدث أكثر إقناعًا في النقاش المهني.
examples: It remains to be seen whether green hydrogen can compete on price with natural gas.
There's a considerable degree of uncertainty surrounding the future cost of electrolysers.
The long-term implications for employment are likely to be significant, particularly in the energy sector.

words.ar: متغيّر مُربِك / عامل خارجي يؤثر في النتائج
words.ex: Anxiety could be a confounding variable affecting both screen use and sleep quality.
Self-reported data on screen time tends to be unreliable, as people often underestimate their usage.
With a sample size of only 200 students, the results may not be representative.
The researchers stopped short of claiming a causal link between social media and insomnia.
Findings from one city's schools are not necessarily generalisable to the entire country.

words.ar: دراسة طولية (تتابع المشاركين على مدى زمني طويل)
words.ex: A longitudinal study would reveal whether sleep patterns change as screen habits evolve.

dialogue.t: Here's the summary: a survey of 500 teenagers found that those using screens for over three hours after 9 p.m. slept, on average, 45 minutes less. What do you make of it?
Well, the data would appear to indicate that late-night screen use and shorter sleep are connected. But correlation doesn't necessarily imply causation.
Meaning what, exactly?
It could work the other way round. Teenagers who already struggle to sleep might simply reach for their phones. Or stress could be a confounding variable driving both.
Fair point. Anything else that concerns you about the methodology?
Yes. One limitation of the study is that it relied on self-reported data, and people are notoriously poor at estimating their screen time.
So should we dismiss the findings?

Not dismiss, but they ought to be treated with caution, given that it's a single snapshot in time. It would be worth investigating whether the same pattern holds in a longitudinal study using objective tracking apps.

grammar.title: Academic hedging with modal verbs
grammar.ar: في تفسير البيانات البحثية نستخدم أفعالًا مساعدة لتخفيف الادعاءات، مثل would appear to بدلًا من shows، وought to be للتوصية المهذبة، وIt would be worth + الفعل بصيغة ing لاقتراح بحث مستقبلي. هذا الأسلوب يعكس الحذر العلمي ويُظهر أن المتحدث يدرك حدود الأدلة. لاحظ أن would هنا لا تدل على الماضي أو الشرط، بل على التحفّظ والتلطيف.
examples: The results would appear to suggest that blue light has a measurable effect on melatonin levels.
These conclusions ought to be treated with caution, given the relatively small sample size.
It would be worth investigating whether the effect differs between boys and girls.

words.ex: The moderator raised a pertinent question about who bears responsibility when AI makes a mistake.
I'd like to qualify my earlier statement: automation won't eliminate all jobs, only certain tasks.
Algorithmic bias can lead recruitment software to unfairly reject qualified candidates.
Clear lines of accountability are essential if AI is used in medical diagnosis.
Job displacement is likely to hit administrative roles hardest in the coming decade.
Ideally, AI should augment human creativity rather than replace it.

dialogue.t: Welcome back to the panel. Our first question: will AI ultimately destroy more jobs than it creates?
That's a pertinent question, and I'd approach it from two angles: the short-term disruption and the long-term restructuring of work.
You mentioned disruption. Are you suggesting mass unemployment is inevitable?
Let me qualify what I said earlier. Disruption doesn't mean permanent loss. Many roles will be transformed, with AI augmenting rather than replacing human workers.
Some artists argue that AI-generated art threatens creativity itself. How would you respond?
The real issue, as I see it, is not whether machines can produce art but rather whether we still value the human intention behind it.
Finally, should AI be making decisions in areas like criminal justice or healthcare?
I'd be reluctant to endorse that without robust safeguards against algorithmic bias and clear accountability. A human must remain responsible for the final decision.

grammar.title: Contrastive focus: not ... but rather / reluctant to ... without
grammar.ar: نستخدم التركيب The real issue is not X but rather Y لإعادة توجيه النقاش من فكرة سطحية إلى جوهر المشكلة، ويجب أن يكون X وY من النوع النحوي نفسه (اسمان أو جملتان). أما I'd be reluctant to + المصدر + without + اسم أو فعل بصيغة ing فيُعبّر عن تحفّظ مشروط بطريقة دبلوماسية. هذه الأساليب مفيدة جدًا في المناظرات واللقاءات الرسمية للتعبير عن موقف دقيق دون حدّة.
examples: The real issue is not the technology itself but rather how it is regulated.
I'd be reluctant to endorse autonomous weapons without binding international agreements.
The question is not whether AI will change education but rather how quickly schools can adapt.

words.ex: My long-term aspiration is to contribute to medical research that genuinely changes lives.
I intend to pursue a degree in environmental engineering, ideally abroad.

words.ar: تكويني؛ ذو أثر عميق في تشكيل الشخصية
words.ex: Spending a summer volunteering was a formative experience that shaped my priorities.

words.ar: يلقى صدى لدى شخص؛ يمسّ وجدانه
words.ex: The idea of serving one's community really resonates with me.
Teaching younger students gives me a real sense of purpose.
I'm driven more by intrinsic curiosity than by the prospect of a high salary.

dialogue.t: So, tell me a little about what you're hoping to study after school.
To be perfectly honest, I've gone back and forth on it, but I've settled on architecture. What really draws me to it is the way it blends creativity with very practical problem-solving.
Interesting. Has that interest been there for a long time?
I've always been fascinated by old buildings, largely because my grandfather used to take me around the historic districts in Jeddah and explain how they kept cool without air conditioning.
And where do you see yourself in, say, ten years?
Looking ahead, I'd ideally like to work on sustainable housing projects, designs that draw on traditional techniques but meet modern needs.
What would you say matters most to you in life?
It's something I've given a great deal of thought to, actually. I'd say integrity. If people can't trust what you say, nothing else you achieve really carries much weight.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences for emphasis
grammar.ar: الجمل المشطورة (Cleft sentences) تُستخدم لإبراز فكرة معيّنة وجعل الإجابة تبدو طبيعية وناضجة. نستخدم بنية What + فاعل + فعل + is/was + المعلومة المهمة، أو بنية It is/was + العنصر المؤكَّد + that/who. هذا الأسلوب يشبه في العربية قولنا: «إنّ ما يجذبني حقاً هو...». احرص على ألا تُكثر منها حتى لا تبدو إجاباتك محفوظة.
examples: What really draws me to medicine is the chance to make a tangible difference.
It was my chemistry teacher who first sparked my interest in research.
What I value most in a friend is honesty, even when it's uncomfortable.

words.ex: This photo of a crowded motorway epitomises the downside of rapid urbanisation.
Social media is a double-edged sword: it connects people but also isolates them.

words.ar: تجاور متناقض؛ وضع أمرين متباينين جنباً إلى جنب
words.ex: The juxtaposition of the ancient mosque and the glass tower is striking.

words.ar: يكون له ثمن؛ يأتي على حساب شيء ما
words.ex: Industrial growth has often come at a cost to the environment.
She made a compelling case for choosing the image of the solar farm.
After some debate, we finally reached a consensus on the two strongest images.

dialogue.t: Let's start by talking about how these pictures reflect different aspects of progress.

What strikes me about this one is the juxtaposition of the farmer with a tablet in the middle of a wheat field. It could be argued that this image represents technology reaching even the most traditional sectors.
True, though I'd say the factory one is more ambiguous. Progress, yes, but it clearly comes at a cost.
Absolutely, it's a double-edged sword. Shall we narrow it down to the images that show both benefits and drawbacks?
Good idea. That leaves the factory, the smartphone users and the space launch.
I'd be tempted to go for the smartphone users, if only because almost everyone can relate to it. It epitomises how progress changes daily life, not just industry.
That's a compelling point. The space launch feels a bit remote by comparison.
So, are we agreed that the smartphone image best captures the theme for a general audience?

grammar.title: Speculating with modals and impersonal structures
grammar.ar: عند وصف الصور والتخمين حول معانيها نستخدم أفعال الاحتمال مثل might / could / must + المصدر للحاضر، و might have / must have + التصريف الثالث للماضي. كما نستخدم التراكيب غير الشخصية مثل It could be argued that... و It would seem that... لتقديم رأي بأسلوب أكاديمي متحفّظ. هذا يجعلك تبدو موضوعياً لا متسرّعاً في الحكم.
examples: The photographer might be trying to highlight the gap between rich and poor.
This town must have changed dramatically over the past few decades.
It could be argued that the image glorifies technology rather than questioning it.

words.ex: Historic sites play a vital role in preserving a nation's collective memory.
AlUla's restoration shows how heritage can be protected and shared with the world.
Governments have a duty to safeguard endangered languages and traditions.
Cities must strike a balance between modern development and conservation.
Oral poetry is part of our intangible cultural heritage.
Shared values underpin a society's sense of identity.

dialogue.t: Your question is: 'How important is it for societies to preserve the past?' You have two minutes.
There are several dimensions to this question, the first being identity. Our heritage underpins how we see ourselves, and without it, a society risks losing its collective memory.
This is perhaps best illustrated by the restoration of Diriyah, which has given young Saudis a much more vivid connection to their history.
Turning now to the economic side, heritage tourism can generate considerable revenue, provided sites are safeguarded rather than overcommercialised.
Another point worth considering is intangible heritage, things like dialects, crafts and oral poetry, which can disappear within a generation if no one records them.
Ultimately, I'd contend that preservation is essential, but societies need to strike a balance so the past informs the future rather than holding it back.
Thank you. Do you think young people today genuinely care about preserving the past?
More than we're given credit for, I'd say, especially when heritage is presented in an engaging, interactive way.

grammar.title: Participle and absolute clauses for cohesion
grammar.ar: تساعد جمل اسم الفاعل والمفعول (participle clauses) على ربط الأفكار بإيجاز وأناقة في الحديث المطوّل. مثلاً: the first being... تعني «وأوّلها هو...»، و Having considered... تعني «بعد أن تناولنا...». الفاعل الضمني يجب أن يكون واضحاً، وإلا فاستخدم بنية مستقلة مثل: The reasons being clear, ... هذه التراكيب تمنح المتحدث طلاقة أكاديمية عالية.
examples: There are two main reasons, the most important being economic sustainability.
Having looked at the cultural side, I'd now like to turn to the economic implications.
Built over three centuries ago, the old town still attracts thousands of visitors.

words.ex: Reformulating a difficult question gives you time to organise your thoughts.

words.ar: فارق دقيق؛ تفصيل دقيق في المعنى
words.ex: A strong answer acknowledges the nuances rather than taking an extreme position.
Whether technology makes us happier is a highly contentious issue.
The answer really hinges on how we define success.
I don't think ambition is inherently good or bad.

words.ar: مسألة قابلة للنقاش ولا حسم فيها
words.ex: Whether exams measure true intelligence remains a moot point.

dialogue.t: Do you think a society can ever be truly fair?
That's a rather thought-provoking question. It largely depends on what we mean by 'fair'. Equal outcomes and equal opportunities are two very different things.
Let's say equal opportunities, then.
In that case, I'd have to say that complete equality is probably unattainable, simply because family background inevitably shapes a child's chances, but societies can narrow the gap considerably.
Is progress always a good thing?
I'm not sure there's a straightforward answer, but I don't believe progress is inherently good. Its value hinges on who benefits and who bears the cost.
Should individuals or governments be responsible for tackling climate change?
If we look at it from a broader perspective, it's a false choice. Individual habits matter, but without policy and investment, personal efforts can only go so far.

grammar.title: Hedging and distancing language
grammar.ar: في الأسئلة المجرّدة يُفضَّل تجنّب الأحكام المطلقة واستخدام لغة التحفّظ (hedging) مثل: tend to، arguably، it would seem that، to some extent. هذه العبارات تُظهر تفكيراً ناضجاً ووعياً بتعقيد القضية. انتبه إلى أنّ العربية تميل أحياناً إلى التعميم القوي، بينما يُقدّر التقييم في امتحان C2 الدقة والاعتدال في التعبير.
examples: It would seem that wealth alone does not guarantee happiness.
Young people arguably face more pressure today than previous generations did.
To some extent, education tends to reproduce existing social inequalities.

words.ex: Economic diversification is one of the central pillars of Vision 2030.

words.ar: عبارات توجيهية تنظّم العرض وترشد المستمع
words.ex: Clear signposting helps the audience follow a complex argument.
The projected number of tourists for 2030 is extremely ambitious.
Major sporting events can catalyse investment in infrastructure.
The growth of local gaming studios is a case in point.
Tourism must be managed carefully to ensure sustainable growth.

dialogue.t: Good morning, everyone. The aim of this presentation is to examine how tourism is contributing to economic diversification under Vision 2030.
I've divided my talk into three sections: the current situation, the main growth drivers, and the challenges ahead.
As the figures illustrate, visitor numbers have risen sharply, with the Red Sea and AlUla projects acting as a case in point.
This brings me to my next point: what is actually catalysing this growth? Simplified e-visas and major events have clearly played a central role.
Turning to the challenges, sustainable growth will depend on protecting fragile ecosystems and training a skilled local workforce.
To sum up, the key takeaway is that tourism is no longer a side sector; it's becoming a genuine pillar of the economy. I'd be happy to take any questions.
Thank you, that was very clearly structured. Could you say a bit more about the workforce training you mentioned?

grammar.title: Nominalisation in academic speech
grammar.ar: التسمية (nominalisation) هي تحويل الأفعال والصفات إلى أسماء، مثل: grow ← growth و diversify ← diversification. يجعل هذا الأسلوب العرض أكثر رسمية وتركيزاً على الأفكار بدلاً من الأشخاص. لكن في العرض الشفهي يجب الموازنة بينه وبين الجمل الفعلية الواضحة حتى لا يصبح الكلام ثقيلاً على السامع.
examples: The expansion of the digital economy has created thousands of new jobs.
The implementation of new regulations led to a significant rise in investment.
There has been a marked increase in female participation in the workforce.

words.ex: I have to concede that my sample size was relatively small.
Could you elaborate on how you collected your data?
Long-term environmental effects were beyond the scope of this study.
A more rigorous analysis would compare several countries.
Her discourse management was excellent: her ideas were coherent and well linked.
Thank you, I'll certainly take that feedback on board.

dialogue.t: You suggested that esports could become a major industry, but didn't you overlook the risks of excessive screen time?
That's an excellent point, and one I perhaps should have addressed more directly. I'd concede that the health implications are significant.
You also seemed to say that traditional sports are declining.
If I could just clarify, what I was trying to convey was that esports is growing faster, not that traditional sports are losing popularity.
How do you think this will affect university admissions policies?
I'm afraid that falls slightly outside the scope of my research, but some universities abroad already offer esports scholarships, so it's a trend worth watching.
Overall, your discourse management was strong, though your analysis of the figures could be more rigorous.
Thank you, I'll take that on board. I'd welcome further discussion on how to strengthen the data section.

grammar.title: Softening with past forms and 'would'
grammar.ar: في الردّ على الأسئلة الصعبة أو النقد نستخدم صيغ الماضي و would لتليين الكلام وإظهار اللباقة، مثل: What I was trying to say... و I would argue... و I was wondering if... الزمن الماضي هنا لا يشير إلى الماضي فعلاً، بل يخلق مسافة مهذّبة. هذا الأسلوب ضروري للحفاظ على نبرة أكاديمية واثقة دون أن تبدو دفاعياً.
examples: What I was trying to suggest was that the data shows a correlation, not causation.
I would argue that the benefits outweigh the risks in the long term.
I was wondering whether you could clarify what you meant by 'sustainable'.

words.ar: وصيّ أو حارس (على التراث أو القيم)
words.ex: Young Saudis increasingly see themselves as custodians of sites like Diriyah rather than mere visitors.

words.ar: التجانس الثقافي، أي ذوبان الثقافات في نمط عالمي واحد
words.ex: Critics warn that cultural homogenization could leave every city looking and sounding the same.
Despite studying abroad, she retained a strong sense of rootedness in her family's traditions.

words.ar: عالمي الطابع، منفتح على ثقافات متعددة
words.ex: Riyadh has developed a remarkably cosmopolitan atmosphere over the past decade.
The revitalization of AlUla has drawn global attention to the Nabataean legacy.
Many teenagers struggle to reconcile their parents' expectations with the lifestyles they see online.

dialogue.t: I've been thinking a lot about this lately. There's an inherent tension between wanting to embrace global trends and wanting to stay true to where we come from.
Do you really see it as a conflict, though? Some would say the two can coexist quite comfortably.
Actually, I'd agree to some extent. Far from eroding our identity, globalization has arguably made us more conscious of it. When tourists flock to AlUla, it reminds us how unique our heritage is.
That's an interesting point. So you think international attention has actually strengthened people's pride?
In many ways, yes. For many of my generation, Diriyah has come to represent not just the past, but a kind of confidence about the future.
But surely there are areas where something is being lost, like dialects or traditional crafts?

Absolutely, and I don't want to romanticize it. It's a question of striking a balance between openness and preservation, and that balance isn't automatic. It takes deliberate effort from families, schools and young people themselves.
So the responsibility falls partly on your generation to act as custodians, then?

grammar.title: Far from + -ing / noun for contrastive emphasis
grammar.ar: نستخدم عبارة Far from متبوعة بفعل بصيغة ‎-ing‎ أو باسم لنفي توقّع شائع بقوة، ثم نقدّم الحقيقة المعاكسة له. وهي تعني تقريبًا «بدلًا من أن... بل على العكس». تُعدّ هذه البنية من سمات الأسلوب الأكاديمي الرفيع، وتأتي غالبًا في بداية الجملة لإبراز التناقض. تنبّه إلى أنّ فاعل الجزأين يجب أن يكون واحدًا.
examples: Far from eroding local customs, tourism has arguably given them a new lease of life.
Far from being a burden, our traditions provide a sense of stability in a fast-changing world.
Far from rejecting modernity, young Saudis are redefining what it means to be modern.

words.ar: التبديل اللغوي، أي التنقّل بين لغتين في الحديث نفسه
words.ex: Code-switching between Arabic and English is second nature for most of my friends.

words.ar: غير قابل للترجمة بدقة إلى لغة أخرى
words.ex: Words like 'tarab' are often described as untranslatable because they carry a whole cultural experience.

words.ar: النسبية اللغوية، أي فرضية أنّ اللغة تؤثّر في طريقة التفكير
words.ex: The theory of linguistic relativity suggests that the language we speak shapes how we perceive reality.

words.ar: فارق دقيق في المعنى أو الدلالة
words.ex: Some of the nuance of a classical Arabic poem inevitably gets lost in translation.
Proverbs in my mother tongue have an emotional resonance that their English equivalents simply lack.

words.ar: يعبّر عن فكرة أو شعور بوضوح ودقة
words.ex: I sometimes find it easier to articulate abstract ideas in English than in Arabic.

dialogue.t: It's something I've noticed about myself for years. I find that when I switch to English, I tend to be more direct, almost blunter, than I would be in Arabic.
Really? Why do you think that is?
Partly it's the language itself. Arabic has so many layers of politeness and indirect expression built in, especially when you're talking to elders.
And what about emotions? Do you feel them differently depending on the language?
Definitely. There are certain concepts that simply don't translate, such as 'ghurba', that feeling of being a stranger far from home. 'Homesickness' doesn't come close.
So expressing that feeling in English must feel a bit incomplete.
Exactly. It's as though I'm wearing someone else's clothes: they fit, but not quite. I'd go so far as to say that I have two slightly different personalities depending on which language I'm using.
That's fascinating. It sounds like there might be some truth to linguistic relativity after all.

grammar.title: As though / as if + unreal past
grammar.ar: نستخدم as though أو as if لتشبيه موقف بموقف آخر. إذا كان التشبيه غير واقعي أو افتراضيًا، نستخدم زمن الماضي حتى لو كنا نتحدث عن الحاضر، ويمكن استخدام were مع جميع الضمائر في الأسلوب الرسمي. أما إذا كان التشبيه محتملًا وواقعيًا، فنستخدم الزمن الطبيعي للجملة. ونستخدم الماضي التام للحديث عن موقف افتراضي في الماضي.
examples: It's as though I were a different person when I speak English.
She talks about Arabic poetry as if it had shaped her entire worldview.
It feels as though some emotions can only exist in one language.

words.ex: Both delegations had to make significant concessions before a draft could be agreed.
Despite their differences, the two sides found common ground on renewable energy research.
For island nations, a firm emissions target is non-negotiable.

words.ar: يخفّف أو يُضعف (اقتراحًا أو بيانًا) حتى يفقد قوته
words.ex: Activists accused the summit of watering down its final statement.
Some delegates resisted any binding commitment that might restrict economic growth.
A phased approach to the energy transition would give developing economies time to adapt.

dialogue.t: Our position is clear: the statement must call for an immediate end to all fossil fuel investment. Anything less would be meaningless.
With all due respect, I'm not entirely convinced that an immediate end is realistic for every country, particularly those whose economies are still heavily reliant on energy exports.
But the science doesn't wait for economies to be ready. We simply don't have the time.

I can see where you're coming from, but a statement that half the delegations refuse to sign won't achieve anything either. Perhaps we could find some common ground on investment in clean technology and carbon capture.
I'd be worried that focusing on technology lets countries delay real action.
That's a fair concern. Would you be open to the idea of a phased approach, with clear deadlines and annual reviews, so there's genuine accountability?
Possibly, as long as the deadlines aren't watered down.
Agreed. And I wonder if we might reconsider the wording of the opening paragraph, so that it recognises both urgency and fairness.

grammar.title: Tentative language for diplomatic distance
grammar.ar: في المواقف الدبلوماسية نستخدم أدوات تخفّف من حدّة الكلام، مثل الأفعال الناقصة might وcould وwould، وصيغة الماضي أو المستمر مع أفعال مثل wonder وhope لإظهار التهذيب لا للدلالة على الزمن. كما نستخدم كلمات مخففة مثل entirely وperhaps وslightly لتجنّب الرفض المباشر. هذا الأسلوب يحافظ على العلاقة ويُبقي باب التفاوض مفتوحًا.
examples: I was wondering if we might revisit the second clause.
Perhaps it would be more productive to focus on what we agree on.
I'm not entirely sure that this proposal would be acceptable to all parties.

words.ar: التهوين المتعمَّد، أي وصف أمر بأقل من حجمه الحقيقي لغرض بلاغي أو فكاهي
words.ex: Describing a sandstorm that grounded every flight as 'a bit breezy' is classic British understatement.

words.ar: بوجه جامد ونبرة جادة رغم أنّ الكلام فكاهي
words.ex: His deadpan delivery made the joke even funnier.

words.ar: على سبيل المزاح الساخر وليس بجدية
words.ex: Her tongue-in-cheek review of the hotel had everyone in stitches.

words.ar: نعمة متخفّية، وتقابلها عبارة «رُبّ ضارةٍ نافعة»
words.ex: Missing the train was a blessing in disguise, since I met an old friend at the station.

words.ar: ساخر بخفة وذكاء، يمزج الطرافة ببعض المرارة
words.ex: She gave a wry smile when the teacher announced yet another surprise test.
The first attempt at cooking kabsa was, to put it mildly, not a success.

dialogue.t: So, in that clip, the man's house is flooded and he says, 'Well, it's not ideal.' What's going on there?
It's understatement. He's being deadpan on purpose. It wasn't exactly a minor inconvenience, to put it mildly.
Exactly. Now, do you have a story where that kind of humour might work?
Actually, yes. Last year I was supposed to give a presentation at a science competition in Jeddah. Little did I know that my laptop would die five minutes before I went on stage.
Oh no. I imagine you were thrilled.
That's one way of looking at it. Needless to say, I wasn't feeling particularly calm. I had to present everything from memory with just a marker and a whiteboard.
And how did it go?
It turned out to be a blessing in disguise, since the judges said my explanation felt far more natural than the slide-heavy presentations. I came second, which, frankly, wasn't too shabby.

grammar.title: Negative inversion: Little did I know...
grammar.ar: عندما نبدأ الجملة بتعبير نفي أو تقييد مثل Little أو Never أو Hardly أو Not only، نعكس ترتيب الفاعل والفعل المساعد كما في السؤال، ونستخدم do أو does أو did إذا لم يوجد فعل مساعد. تضيف هذه البنية تشويقًا ودرامية للقصة، وهي شائعة في السرد والكتابة الرسمية. مثال: بدلًا من I knew little نقول Little did I know.
examples: Little did I know that this small mistake would change my entire summer.
Never had I felt so embarrassed in front of an audience.
Hardly had we arrived when the power went out.

words.ar: يُديم أو يرسّخ (صورة نمطية أو فكرة خاطئة)
words.ex: Action films often perpetuate the image of the Arab world as a desert battlefield.

words.ar: اختزالي، يبسّط واقعًا معقدًا بشكل مُخلّ
words.ex: It is reductive to define an entire region by a handful of news headlines.

words.ar: الاستشراق، أي تصوير الشرق بنظرة غربية نمطية وغرائبية
words.ex: Edward Said's work on Orientalism remains essential reading for anyone studying media representation.

words.ar: رواية مضادة أو بديلة تتحدى الرواية السائدة
words.ex: Saudi filmmakers are building a powerful counter-narrative through festivals and streaming platforms.

words.ar: التمثيل الشكلي، أي إشراك فئة بشكل رمزي دون تمثيل حقيقي
words.ex: Including a single Arab character with no depth is little more than tokenism.

words.ar: تصوير دقيق ومتوازن يراعي التعقيد والتنوع
words.ex: The series was praised for its nuanced portrayal of family life in Riyadh.

dialogue.t: When you watch international films set in the Middle East, what strikes you most?
Honestly, the portrayal tends to perpetuate the same tired images: endless desert, conflict, and characters who are either villains or victims.
Some would argue that's simply what makes for dramatic storytelling.

Perhaps, but what is often overlooked is the everyday reality: students, entrepreneurs, artists, women leading companies. This reductive image fails to capture the diversity and dynamism of a country like Saudi Arabia.
So whose job is it to change that? Hollywood's?
Partly. Content creators bear some responsibility for what they choose to show, especially when they reach millions of viewers. But we can't just wait for others to tell our story.
What would you suggest young people actually do?

If we are to challenge these stereotypes, we need to produce our own content, in English as well as Arabic, and engage respectfully with international audiences. A credible counter-narrative has to be honest, not just promotional.

grammar.title: If + be to + infinitive (conditions of necessity)
grammar.ar: نستخدم البنية If + subject + be to + infinitive للتعبير عن هدف أو غاية، ثم نذكر الشرط اللازم لتحقيقها في الجملة الرئيسية، وغالبًا مع need to أو must أو have to. المعنى: «إذا أردنا حقًا أن...، فعلينا أن...». هذه البنية رسمية وتُستخدم بكثرة في النقاشات الأكاديمية والخطابات المقنعة.
examples: If we are to challenge harmful stereotypes, we need to tell our own stories.
If the media is to regain public trust, it must report with far greater accuracy.
If young people were to take the lead online, the narrative could shift within a decade.

words.ar: يُيسّر أو يدير (نقاشًا أو عملية) دون فرض رأيه
words.ex: A good moderator facilitates the discussion rather than dominating it.

words.ar: يقاطع بإدخال تعليق قصير أثناء حديث الآخرين
words.ex: Sorry to interject, but I think we're drifting off topic.

words.ar: إجماع أو توافق عام في الرأي
words.ex: By the end of the session, the group had reached a broad consensus on the need for empathy.

words.ar: يعيد صياغة كلام شخص آخر بأسلوبه الخاص
words.ex: Let me paraphrase what you've said to make sure I've got it right.

words.ar: يستطرد أو يخرج عن الموضوع الرئيسي
words.ex: I don't want to digress too far, but this links to what we discussed earlier.
The panel brought together divergent views on whether global citizenship weakens national identity.

dialogue.t: Welcome, everyone. Today's question is what it actually means to be a global citizen. Lena, perhaps we could hear your take on that first.
(as Lena, from Germany) For me, it's mostly about responsibility, like caring about climate change or refugees even if they don't affect you directly.
Thank you. If I've understood you correctly, you're suggesting that global citizenship is primarily an ethical commitment rather than a legal status. Kenji, would you agree?
(as Kenji, from Japan) Partly, but I worry it can become a fashionable label. Some people travel a lot and call themselves global citizens, but they never really engage with local cultures.
That's an important distinction. Building on what was just said, does that mean genuine global citizenship requires humility and curiosity, not just mobility?
(as Lena) Yes, and also knowing your own culture well. You can't respect others if you don't understand where you come from.

Let's not lose sight of that point, because it connects both views. To draw these threads together, it seems we agree that being a global citizen means combining ethical responsibility with real cultural engagement, starting from a secure sense of one's own identity.
(as Kenji) I think that's a fair summary.

grammar.title: Participle clauses for linking ideas
grammar.ar: تُستخدم الجمل الوصفية بصيغة اسم الفاعل (‎-ing‎) أو اسم المفعول (التصريف الثالث) أو Having + التصريف الثالث لربط الأفكار بإيجاز وأناقة، بدلًا من استخدام because أو after أو when. تضفي هذه البنية طابعًا احترافيًا على إدارة النقاشات والكتابة الأكاديمية. يجب أن يكون فاعل الجملة الوصفية هو نفسه فاعل الجملة الرئيسية.
examples: Building on Lena's point, I'd like to ask whether responsibility has limits.
Having heard both perspectives, we can now look for areas of agreement.
Seen from a different angle, global citizenship might actually strengthen local identity.

units.t: Precision in Argument: Academic Debate and Critical Reasoning
units.ar: الدقة في الحِجاج: النقاش الأكاديمي والتفكير النقدي
units.cando: Can construct and sustain a sophisticated, well-structured argument on complex academic issues, conceding, refuting and qualifying points with precise hedging and emphasis so that subtle distinctions of meaning are conveyed effortlessly.
lessons: Hedging and Degrees of Certainty
Learner discusses with the tutor whether standardized university entrance exams such as Qudurat and Tahsili accurately predict academic success, calibrating how strongly each claim is made.

It would be somewhat simplistic to claim that ...; There is a strong case to be made that ..., although ...; The evidence would seem to suggest that ...; I'd be inclined to argue that ..., albeit with certain reservations.
Conceding and Counter-Arguing Gracefully
In a formal university-style seminar role-play, learner acknowledges the tutor's opposing view on mandatory volunteering for school graduation before dismantling it.
Granted, ...; nevertheless, ...; While I take your point that ..., it doesn't necessarily follow that ...; Much as I appreciate ..., I'd question whether ...; Be that as it may, ...
Exposing Logical Fallacies
Tutor presents flawed arguments drawn from social media debates; learner identifies false dilemmas, slippery slopes and hasty generalizations and articulates why they fail.

That argument rests on the assumption that ..., which is by no means self-evident; To frame it as either ... or ... is a false dichotomy; There's no causal link between ... and ...; That's a sweeping generalization that overlooks ...
Emphasis Through Inversion and Cleft Structures
Learner delivers a persuasive two-minute argument on whether Arabic or English should be the primary language of instruction in Saudi universities, using marked structures for rhetorical force.
Not only does ..., but it also ...; Rarely do we consider ...; What concerns me most is ...; It is precisely because ... that ...; Under no circumstances should ...; Only when ... will ...
Synthesizing Multiple Perspectives
Learner summarizes three contrasting expert opinions on remote versus in-person learning provided by the tutor, then weighs them to reach a nuanced conclusion of their own.

Whereas X contends that ..., Y takes a rather more cautious stance, arguing ...; What these views have in common is ...; Taken together, these perspectives point to ...; On balance, I'm persuaded that ..., provided that ...
Full Oxford-Style Debate

Learner and tutor hold a timed formal debate on the motion 'This house believes that artificial intelligence will do more harm than good to education', including opening statement, rebuttal and closing.

I rise to propose / oppose the motion that ...; My opponent has conveniently glossed over ...; Allow me to address the central claim that ...; Far from ..., the evidence clearly indicates ...; In closing, I would urge you to consider ...

units.t: Science, Ethics and the Future: Discussing Innovation Responsibly
units.ar: العلم والأخلاق والمستقبل: مناقشة الابتكار بمسؤولية
units.cando: Can discuss abstract and specialized scientific and ethical topics with fluency and precision, speculating about hypothetical outcomes, evaluating risks and benefits, and reformulating complex ideas so that a non-specialist listener can follow them.
lessons: Speculating About Technological Futures
Learner and tutor speculate on how smart cities such as NEOM might reshape daily life, work and privacy by 2050.
Were ... to become widespread, we might well see ...; It's not inconceivable that ...; In all likelihood, ... will have ... by the time ...; Should ... fail, the consequences could be ...
Medical Ethics and Genetic Research
Learner explores the ethical boundaries of gene editing for disease prevention, considering Islamic bioethical principles alongside international scientific perspectives.
The crux of the matter is whether ...; One could argue that ... is justifiable insofar as ...; There's a fine line between ... and ...; From an ethical standpoint, the key concern is ...
